title: Why Do We Take the People We Love for Granted?
metaTitle: Why Do We Take the People We Love for Granted?
metaDescription: Taking loved ones for granted is a predictable result of adaptation and safety, and research suggests deliberate appreciation can counteract it.
keyFinding: Taking the people we love for granted is a predictable result of two ordinary processes — getting used to what is reliable, and relaxing our guard with those we feel safest with — and research on gratitude suggests it can be partly reversed by deliberate appreciation.
honestAnswer: Mostly because of two normal processes, not because we care less. The first is adaptation: just as we stop noticing any constant in our lives, we get used to a reliable partner, friend, or family member and stop registering them the way we did at first. The second is safety: we tend to let our guard down — and sometimes let our worst out — with the people whose love we feel most sure of, precisely because we assume it is secure.

Both of these are predictable rather than a character flaw, and both appear to be reversible. Research on gratitude in relationships suggests that deliberately noticing and expressing appreciation can interrupt the drift and bring attention back to people who have quietly become part of the background.
whatDataShows: The clearest explanation comes from hedonic adaptation — the well-documented tendency to adjust to circumstances over time so that their emotional impact fades. It is usually discussed for things like income or possessions, but it applies to relationships too: a partner or friend who once felt remarkable becomes the new normal, and the brain gives a steady, expected presence less attention than a novel or uncertain one.

On the relationship side, Sara Algoe's 'find-remind-bind' theory of gratitude describes how feeling grateful in a relationship helps people notice a good partner or friend ('find'), refreshes their appreciation of someone already in their life ('remind'), and strengthens the bond ('bind'). The implication is that gratitude is partly a mechanism that counteracts the natural fading of attention toward people we are used to.

There is also the familiar pattern of 'saving our best behaviour for strangers.' We tend to be more polite, patient, and accommodating with acquaintances and colleagues than with those closest to us, in part because we assume close relationships can absorb our irritability and unguarded moments. Research on politeness and familiarity is consistent with the idea that perceived security loosens the effort we put into everyday courtesy at home.
whyItFeelsDifferent: It feels like indifference when it is usually adaptation. Because the fading of attention happens gradually and invisibly, it is easy to mistake 'I have stopped noticing' for 'I have stopped caring,' even though the underlying feeling may be intact. The signal simply got quieter because it became constant.

It also feels paradoxical that we treat the people we love most with the least visible effort. But that is partly the point: the more secure a bond feels, the safer it seems to relax, vent, and skip the small courtesies we extend to people whose goodwill we are less sure of. Security, which is genuinely valuable, has this predictable side effect.

And the cost is asymmetric in a way that is easy to miss. The person being taken for granted often feels the inattention clearly, while the person doing it barely registers a change, because for them nothing dramatic happened — they simply stopped noticing a constant. That mismatch is why it so often goes unspoken until it has built up.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The most direct counter is deliberate appreciation. Research on gratitude in relationships suggests that regularly noticing and expressing specific things you value about a partner, friend, or family member is associated with feeling more connected and more committed — for both the person expressing it and the person receiving it. The 'find-remind-bind' framing positions this as a way of refreshing attention that adaptation has dulled.

Specificity and sincerity seem to matter more than frequency or grand gestures. Naming a particular thing someone did, rather than offering a generic 'thanks,' tends to land more strongly in the research, likely because it signals genuine attention rather than routine. The aim is to re-notice the person, not to perform appreciation.

Extending to close relationships the everyday courtesy we reflexively give strangers is another low-cost lever. Because we tend to under-apply politeness and patience precisely where we feel safest, consciously offering the people we love the same small consideration we give acquaintances directly addresses the 'best behaviour for strangers' pattern.
whatDoesNotHelp: Waiting to 'feel' more appreciative before acting on it tends not to work, because the whole problem is that adaptation has quieted the feeling. The research on gratitude suggests the noticing and expressing often comes first and helps revive the attention, rather than the other way around.

Grand, occasional gestures — a big anniversary, an expensive gift — do less to reverse the drift than the data on small, specific, repeated appreciation would predict. A single large gesture is itself something people adapt to, while consistent everyday attention is what most directly counteracts the fading.

Blaming yourself or your partner as uncaring usually misreads the situation. Treating an ordinary, near-universal byproduct of adaptation and security as a personal failing tends to add guilt or conflict without addressing the actual mechanism, which is about attention rather than the depth of the underlying bond.
realNumbersInContext: This is more a 'why' question than a 'how many' question, so the honest framing is mechanistic rather than statistical. Hedonic adaptation is one of the most replicated patterns in wellbeing research, and it offers the clearest explanation for why a reliable, valued person fades into the background over time.

The gratitude side rests largely on experimental and longitudinal studies in psychology rather than large population datasets, and the effects, while reasonably consistent, are modest. The dependable takeaway is directional: deliberate, specific appreciation is associated with feeling more connected, which makes it a plausible and low-cost counter to a predictable problem rather than a guaranteed fix.

faqs.question: Does taking loved ones for granted mean I love them less?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. It is usually adaptation rather than declining feeling — we stop noticing a reliable presence the way we stop noticing any constant. The underlying care can be intact even when the everyday attention to it has quietly faded.

faqs.question: Why do we treat strangers better than the people closest to us?
faqs.answer: Partly because we feel safe with those we love and assume their goodwill can absorb our unguarded moments. Research on politeness and familiarity is consistent with the idea that perceived security loosens the small courtesies we readily extend to acquaintances.

faqs.question: Can you actually reverse taking someone for granted?
faqs.answer: The research on gratitude suggests you can partly counteract it. Deliberately noticing and naming specific things you value about someone is associated with feeling more connected and committed, for both people. Sara Algoe's 'find-remind-bind' theory describes gratitude as a way of refreshing dulled attention.

faqs.question: Do big gestures fix this?
faqs.answer: Less than you might expect. The evidence favours small, specific, repeated appreciation over occasional grand gestures, partly because people adapt to a single large gesture too. Consistent everyday attention is what most directly counters the fading.

faqs.question: Is this just human nature, or something I'm doing wrong?
faqs.answer: It is largely a predictable byproduct of adaptation and feeling secure, not a personal failing. Treating it as a character flaw tends to add guilt without addressing the real mechanism, which is about attention rather than the depth of the bond.
